items.bodyEn: Totsuka lay about ten and a half ri (41 kilometers) from Nihonbashi, a full day's walk, so travelers who left Edo before dawn usually slept here first and the town lived on its inns. Hiroshige's print 'Motomachi Fork' shows a rider swinging off his horse at a teahouse beside a stone post that reads 'left: Kamakura road'.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō 1833–34: Totsuka Motomachi Fork; Shukuson taigaichō

items.bodyEn: 'Getting up early is worth three mon.' A mon was the smallest Edo copper coin, so the proverb promises a small but certain profit for the early riser. Travelers lived by it: a day on the road began in the dark so you reached the next town in daylight. The last word is also written 得, 'gain'.
items.ja: {早起|はやお}きは{三文|さんもん}の{徳|とく}
items.kana: はやおきはさんもんのとく

items.titleEn: Snack Time at the Eighth Bell
items.bodyEn: Edo Japan counted the hours by bells, from nine down to four: 九つ at noon and midnight, then 八つ, 七つ, 六つ. The eighth bell, 八つ時, rang around two in the afternoon, when people took a light meal; that meal became お八つ, today's おやつ. Travelers' 七つ立ち, 'setting out at seven', meant leaving around four in the morning.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien; Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entry おやつ (お八つ); Edo-period bell hours

items.bodyEn: Japanese counts with two number sets. Sino-Japanese いち・に・さん does most counting, but four and seven each borrow a second reading from the native set, よん and なな: し sounds like 死, death, and しち is easily misheard as いち. So よんじゅう rather than しじゅう, yet 四月 is always しがつ. The native ひとつ・ふたつ・みっつ still counts things up to ten.
